name: Senate Rejection of League of Nations
subject: us-history

lesson.title: The Vote That Kept America Out
lesson.summary: The U.S. Senate twice refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, and with it the League of Nations, dealing a fatal blow to Woodrow Wilson's vision of American leadership in a new world order.
lesson.body:
When Woodrow Wilson returned from Paris in 1919 with the Treaty of Versailles under his arm, he believed he had won more than an end to the war. Tucked into the treaty was the covenant of the League of Nations, an international body meant to prevent future wars through collective security and diplomacy. Wilson had personally fought for the League at the peace conference, and he saw it as the crowning achievement of his presidency. But bringing the treaty home was only half the job. Under the Constitution, no treaty becomes binding until two thirds of the Senate approves it, and that requirement gave Wilson's opponents enormous leverage.

The chief obstacle was Henry Cabot Lodge, a Massachusetts Republican who chaired the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Lodge did not lead a single unified bloc. A small group of senators known as the Irreconcilables, including William Borah of Idaho and Hiram Johnson of California, opposed the treaty in any form, fearing any League membership would drag the United States into future European conflicts. A larger group of Reservationists, led by Lodge himself, were willing to accept the treaty only with changes. Their biggest target was Article X of the League covenant, which called on member nations to help defend one another against aggression. Lodge and his allies argued that Article X would commit American troops to overseas wars without the explicit consent of Congress, which the Constitution alone empowers to declare war. This was fundamentally a fight about federalism and the separation of powers: who gets to decide when the United States goes to war, an international council or the elected representatives of the American people.

Wilson refused to accept Lodge's reservations, viewing them as a betrayal of the treaty's spirit. Rather than compromise, he took his case directly to the American public, embarking on an exhausting cross country speaking tour in September 1919. The strain proved too much. Wilson collapsed after a speech in Pueblo, Colorado, on September 25, 1919, and a week later, back in Washington, he suffered a massive stroke that left him partially paralyzed and largely isolated from governing for the rest of his term. With Wilson incapacitated and unwilling to bend, and Lodge unwilling to accept the treaty unamended, the Senate voted the treaty down in November 1919 and again in March 1920. The United States never joined the League of Nations. It eventually made a separate peace with Germany through a 1921 resolution signed by President Warren Harding, and the League limped forward without its most powerful potential member, a weakness that would haunt international diplomacy for the next two decades.
